claims.text: By default the API server stores plain-text representations of resources, including Secrets, in etcd, with no at-rest encryption.

Encryption at rest is configured on the kube-apiserver: --encryption-provider-config names an EncryptionConfiguration file listing resources and providers; by default the file is loaded once, at startup; etcd never sees the key.
claims.source_hint: encrypt-data.md lines 58-60 and 'Configure automatic reloading' (lines 713-717); kube-apiserver.md flag reference

claims.text: The first provider in the list encrypts resources written to storage; when reading, each provider that matches the stored data tries, in order, to decrypt it.
The identity provider writes resources as-is without encryption; listed after secretbox, it lets the API server read Secrets stored unencrypted before the change.
claims.source_hint: encrypt-data.md providers table (identity row, lines 224-235) and line 441 comment

claims.text: The secretbox provider encrypts with a 32-byte key given in base64 in the EncryptionConfiguration file (keys list with name and secret).
claims.source_hint: encrypt-data.md providers table, secretbox row (lines 298-305); scripts/dev-secrets.sh lines 86-106 @ stage-3

claims.text: A Secret written with secretbox and key key1 is stored in etcd with the prefix k8s:enc:secretbox:v1:key1:, naming the provider and the key.
claims.source_hint: encrypt-data.md 'Verifying that data is encrypted' (prefix k8s:enc:aescbc:v1:, line 574); outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/encryption-at-rest.txt

claims.text: Before encryption is configured, a Secret read straight from etcd starts with k8s followed by a non-printable byte, and its value is readable in it (shown by the script as 'k8s.').
An etcd snapshot copies what etcd stores, so Secrets encrypted at rest are encrypted bytes in the snapshot as well.

claims.text: Enabling encryption does not encrypt Secrets already stored; they are encrypted only when written again. kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces -o json | kubectl replace -f - rewrites all Secrets with the same data.
claims.source_hint: encrypt-data.md 'Ensure all relevant data are encrypted' (lines 590-607)

claims.text: Reads through the API server return decrypted values: kubectl get secret still returns the value to any caller RBAC allows, because the API server decrypts with the key it holds.
claims.source_hint: encrypt-data.md (encryption applies to data stored in etcd); outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/encryption-at-rest.txt last command

claims.text: The script first runs scripts/dev-secrets.sh, then adds --encryption-provider-config and a hostPath volume mounting the node's /etc/kubernetes/enc into the kube-apiserver static Pod's container; the kubelet then restarts the API server with the flag.
claims.source_hint: scripts/k8s/encryption-at-rest.sh line 7 and lines 29-47 @ stage-3; encrypt-data.md (API server as static Pod, prerequisites lines 38-40); static Pod docs

claims.text: A locally managed key protects against an etcd compromise but not a host compromise: the key is on the host in the EncryptionConfiguration file, so a copy of the node's disk (which also holds etcd's data folder /var/lib/etcd) holds the key too.

The kms provider relies on a key held by a key service outside Kubernetes that encrypts or decrypts on request, so that key is not on the node's disk; an attacker needs both etcd and that service to read the values.

When a key service outside the cluster exists, kms is the stronger choice; without one, a local secretbox key still protects etcd copies and snapshots taken off the node, and a disk that leaves your hands should be wiped.

In the lab, kubectl replace -f - read the Secrets from the pipe and rewrote 3 across all namespaces (the two lab Secrets plus one the cluster already had), after which lab-before was stored encrypted.
